newsitem.title: USA: Researcher lists new product duds, winners.
newsitem.headline: Researcher lists new product duds, winners.

text.p: Vegetable-flavored gummy bears and soda with colored gel capsules flopped. But no-drip window cleaner, tortilla chips with almost no fat and reusable paper towels were hits, a new product survey found.
Acupoll Research Inc. asked 1,200 women to examine pictures and descriptions of more than 400 products introduced this year and rate their value and "purchase probability."
The women, the main shoppers for their households, did not actually test the products but had strong opinions about what they were likely to buy, the Cincinnati-based new product testing firm said.

Women gave a thumbs-up to Doritos Max tortilla chips, which have one gram of fat per serving compared to seven grams for traditional chips, manufacturer Frito-Lay said. The chips are made with olestra, which critics say may cause intestinal discomfort. The fat substitute has been approved for use in some snack foods by the Food and Drug Administration.

Other winners included Windex No-Drip, which does not trickle down the window, according to SC Johnson Wax, reusable Bounty paper towels from Procter & Gamble Co., and J.M. Smucker Co.'s shortening and oil replacement made with corn syrup, apple puree and pectin, a gel used in jellies and jams.
Phyto-Bears from Mannatech Inc., made from brussels sprouts, turnips and other vegetables. While they look like gummy bears, at $19.50 a box, few surveyed said they would buy.
Clearly Canadian Beverage Corp.'s Orbitz beverage, with colorful gel capsules floating in it, was fun but a little too weird for the women surveyed, Acupoll said.
And Big Head Co.'s Coffee Cola, cold coffee and carbonated cola in flavors including Butter Rumba and Decafanilla, pushed the envelope "a little too far," the research firm said.
Some of the products were available nationwide while others were still being tested or were available regionally.
Acupoll's annual "Pure Gold/Fool's Gold" list is compiled with Marketing Intelligence Ltd., a new product tracking firm, and is not connected with any manufacturer, Acupoll said.
